title: Targeted search: finding the clients that fit your service for Plastering
audience: Plastering contractors in any service business who want more work from clients that suit their service, their area and their job size, such as builders, renovators and property managers.
learningOutcomes: Build a prospect list scored against written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need.
Identify public signals that a plastering need is starting, and explain why each one is a reasonable reason to make contact.
Write a first approach that makes one specific, verifiable observation, offers one small next step, and can be declined easily.

instruction.heading: Decide what plastering work you want before you look for it
instruction.body: Targeted search starts with a clear picture of the work you want more of. Write down the plastering types you do well (room replasters, ceiling work, patch repairs, render), the price range you can sustain, the suburbs you can reach without losing money on travel, and how often each kind of client needs plastering. A builder who sends you a steady stream of stages on a route you already run is worth more to a small plasterer than one large job across town. These criteria are the filter for everything that follows. Business.gov.au suggests writing one profile for each customer segment before you choose a target market (How to identify your target market, 24 September 2024).

instruction.heading: Build a scored prospect list
instruction.body: Keep every candidate in one list, with a fit column and a status column. Score each prospect as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, against the written criteria. Ask whether it sits inside your service area, whether it has a repeat need, whether you can reach the person who makes the buying decision, and whether the job falls within the licence and insurance you hold. Builders, renovation companies, property managers and strata managers are examples of prospects that some plasterers serve, but add a prospect only when it passes the criteria. Record the date each entry was added and where its details came from. Before you contact anyone, confirm the scope, your capacity and the deadline, as Business Queensland advises before sending a quote. Keep only business contact details published for business use. Do not use bought or harvested contact lists. ACMA's guidance says that buying a list does not remove the need to show consent (Spam Act obligations page, last updated 28 March 2019; older source).

instruction.heading: Watch for signals that a plastering need is starting
instruction.body: A signal is a public event that makes a plastering need more likely in the near future. Examples include a public notice of planned building works, a new development approved on a street you already serve, or a planning application on a council register. Victoria's Buying for Victoria portal lists current and past tenders and lets suppliers set alerts, and each agency publishes an annual plan of what it intends to buy. Some councils publish planning permit registers with suburb and status fields, such as the City of Casey register on Victoria's open data portal, so check the register for your own council. Victoria also publishes building permit activity, which records each permit's location, estimated cost and issue date, and can be filtered by suburb or postcode. Use that aggregated activity to decide where to market. Do not use the address of an individual property to contact its owner or occupier. Use signals to decide when to make contact, not to build a profile of individuals.

instruction.heading: Make a first approach that is specific and easy to decline
instruction.body: A useful first message does three things. It states how you came to know about the works or the project. It makes one specific observation you can verify from public view or from the business's own published material, such as a notice about works. It then offers one small next step, such as a written quote for a defined area or a fifteen-minute call. Keep the message short, do not overstate what you know, and make it simple to say no. The ACCC's 2026 review of unsolicited selling found that many approaches were pressured or misleading and that many salespeople did not identify themselves, so an honest, specific message that names you is a practical advantage as well as a compliance step.

instruction.heading: Follow up on a fixed schedule and stop when asked
instruction.body: Decide in advance how many follow-ups you will send and how far apart they will be. A common pattern is one reminder after a week and one final message after a further two weeks, then a pause. Stopping is part of the approach. If a prospect says no, or asks you to stop, remove them from the list at once and record the request with its date. At the end of each month, review which fit tier and which signal produced the replies that became paid work, and move your effort toward them. Silence is not consent to keep contacting someone.

procedure: Write the plastering job, area, price and repeat-need criteria for the work you want.
Build the prospect list and score each entry as strong fit, possible fit or not a fit, with a reason.
Choose two or three public signals to watch and note the date each one is seen.
Write one first message for each fit tier, with a stated source, one verifiable observation and one small next step.
Check each message against the electronic message rules and the licence rules for the job before sending.
Send to strong-fit prospects first, then follow up on the fixed schedule.
Remove anyone who asks you to stop, and review the results at the end of the month.

workedExamples.situation: A plasterer covers three suburbs. A public notice goes up about planned building works at a multi-unit site in one of them. The builder's business email address is published on the company's contact page.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Should the plasterer send a sales message to the builder now, and what should it contain?
workedExamples.reasoning: The plasterer should not send a sales email just because the builder's address is published. ACMA's Spam Act overview says that publishing a business address does not by itself permit commercial messages, so the plasterer first checks whether the builder has agreed to receive them or has invited contact. If neither applies, the plasterer waits for an invitation or uses a route the builder has agreed to. A phone call to a registered number is limited by Do Not Call Register rules, so the register is checked before any telemarketing call. Any message that does go out names the notice, says how the business learned of it, offers one specific plastering stage it could handle, and asks one question. The plasterer does not contact individual owners or tenants using private details, and does not enter the site without an invitation.

equipmentAndPpe: Prospect list in a spreadsheet or notebook, with fit and status columns
Written fit criteria for service area, job size and repeat need
Message templates checked against the electronic message rules
No PPE is needed for desk work; any site visit follows the site's own safety rules

commonErrors.error: Sending the same message to everyone on a broad list at once.
commonErrors.prevention: Score the list first, write one message for each fit tier, and start with the strong-fit tier.

commonErrors.error: Using private information about an individual to make contact.
commonErrors.prevention: Use only contact details published for business use, or details the person has given you for this purpose.

commonErrors.error: Pitching a plastering service that you are not licensed or insured to deliver at that job value.
commonErrors.prevention: Check the state licence rule and your insurance before outreach, and remove that service from the message.

commonErrors.error: Following up without a limit, or continuing after a request to stop.
commonErrors.prevention: Set a fixed number of follow-ups and a stop rule, and record every stop request.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Do not offer a plastering service in outreach unless you hold the licence or registration that the state where the work is done requires for that job value and trade mix. Licence rules differ between states and territories, and the thresholds are not the same. This lesson does not grant any licence.

Commercial electronic messages, including email and text, are regulated by the Spam Act 2003 (Cth). ACMA's avoid-spam guidance says marketing messages need consent, that consent should be recorded, and that unsubscribe requests must be honoured within five working days. The Act text was not read for this lesson, so check it before sending.

Information on a public listing or a public notice does not by itself permit contact about anything. If the Privacy Act applies to your business, OAIC's guidance on direct marketing says public information is not exempt from the direct-marketing rules. Whether the Act applies to a small business is unconfirmed in this draft. Use only contact details published for business use, keep them secure, and stop using them when someone objects.

qualityStandard: Every prospect on the list has a fit score, a reason for that score and a recorded source for its contact details.
Every first message contains one verifiable observation and one small, easy-to-decline next step.
No contact is made using private information, and every stop request is recorded and actioned.
documentationEvidence: Prospect list with fit score, reason, status, source and date added.
Signal log with the date each public signal was seen.
Stop-request record with the date it was actioned.
summary: Define the plastering work you want first, then filter prospects against that definition.
Watch public signals, and never use private information to make contact.
Keep the first approach specific and easy to decline, and stop when asked.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which prospect should you contact first?
options: A one-off job well outside your service area, because it looks large
A builder with several stages inside your service area that you already visit
Any business that has a website, because it probably spends money on plastering

knowledgeChecks.question: A public notice shows planned building works in your area. What is the most appropriate first step?
options: Contact the builder by a route that the electronic message and do-not-call rules allow
Message each owner using their private contact details and ask them to sign up for the works
Go onto the site to look at the work before making contact, and ask the crew what they are doing

knowledgeChecks.question: Before you send a commercial email to a prospect, what should you do?
options: Check that the message is short enough to read on a phone and has a fun subject line
Ask the prospect to like your social media page first, then send the message
Confirm the consent and unsubscribe requirements in current ACMA guidance and the Spam Act before sending

officialReferences.title: Avoid sending spam (ACMA)
officialReferences.covers: Read 2026-11-09 via the CP-01 research: a business needs consent before sending marketing messages, and consent must be recorded; each message must identify the sender and include correct contact details; every commercial message must include an unsubscribe option that works for at least 30 days and is honoured within 5 working days. Does not cover privacy law. Publisher: ACMA.

officialReferences.title: Australian Privacy Principles guidelines (OAIC)
officialReferences.covers: Lists the APP chapters and says the Act covers organisations with annual turnover above $3 million and some other organisations. Small-business coverage and consent detail are UNCONFIRMED because the full PDF was not read. Publisher: OAIC.
